## Incident Report — STRRAT RAT Infection

**Case:** mta-2024-07-30 | **Capture window:** 2024-07-30 06:38:48 – 06:48:34 UTC (585.7 s) | **File:** `2024-07-30-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (SHA256 `c48854c24223cf7b4e9880ea72a21a877e4138e4ce36df7b7656e5c6c4043f68`)

### Victim host
| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 | 172.16.1.66 |
| MAC | 00:1e:64:ec:f3:08 |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-SKBR25F |
| Logged-in domain user | ccollier (domain: WIRESHARKWORKSHOP.ONLINE, confirmed via Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString and via the C2 beacon field) |
| Domain controller (for reference) | WIRESHARK-WS-DC.wiresharkworkshop.online — 172.16.1.4 |

### Malware family
**STRRAT** (Java-based RAT/"fauxware" RAT). **Signature-confirmed**, not behavioral: the C2 protocol carries the literal, unencrypted field `STRRAT` as the second pipe-delimited token in every beacon, which is STRRAT's known plaintext check-in format:

```
ping|STRRAT|<botID>|<hostname>|<user>|<OS>|<arch>|<AV product>|<base64 active-window title>|<version>|<country>|<installed?>|<idle time>
```

Observed literal sample (frame 9067, tcp.stream 83):
`ping|STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|Microsoft Windows 11 Pro|64-bit|Windows Defender||1.6|US:United States|Not Installed|1 Sec`

Bot ID: `1BE8292C`. STRRAT version string: `1.6`. AV reported by the malware itself: Windows Defender.

### Indicators of Compromise

**C2 endpoint**
- `141.98.10.79:12132` (TCP) — plaintext STRRAT beacon protocol, single persistent stream (tcp.stream 83), 411 packets over the full capture, beaconing every ~5 seconds from T+77s onward. No domain/SNI associated (raw IP:port, no TLS).

**Supporting/staging infrastructure (delivery chain, in time order)**
- `github.com` → 140.82.113.3:443 (TLS, T+64.2s) — 9.9 KB
- `objects.githubusercontent.com` → 185.199.110.133:443 (TLS, T+64.9s) — 833 KB downloaded to host (consistent with a GitHub-hosted release/raw payload fetch — encrypted, filename/hash not recoverable from this capture)
- `repo1.maven.org` → 199.232.196.209:443 (TLS, 3 parallel streams, T+68.0s) — 8.9 MB downloaded to host (Java/Maven dependency resolution, consistent with the STRRAT jar bootstrapping its runtime libraries)
- STRRAT C2 beaconing to 141.98.10.79:12132 begins at T+77s, ~9 seconds after the Maven downloads complete — this is the infection/execution chain: GitHub payload fetch → Maven dependency pull → STRRAT jar execution → C2 beacon start.

**Behavioral IOC (not malware-specific but corroborating a loader/infostealer pattern)**
- `ip-api.com` (208.95.112.1) — `GET /json/` with a spoofed Chrome User-Agent (`Mozilla/5.0 ... Chrome/73.0.3683.86`) from a Windows host issuing raw HTTP rather than a browser — public-IP/geolocation self-check, a common pre-C2 recon step for loaders and RATs. Response confirmed geolocation lookup returned (Austin, TX, US).

**No transferred files were recoverable in cleartext.** All payload-bearing transfers (GitHub, Maven, Oracle Java update) rode over TLS; the capture contains no decryption keys and no plaintext file bodies, so no filenames or SHA256 hashes for the dropped jar/binary can be grounded in this traffic. The only cleartext-observed application data is the STRRAT C2 protocol strings themselves and the two benign HTTP exchanges (`www.msftconnecttest.com/connecttest.txt`, `ip-api.com/json/`).

### Summary
DESKTOP-SKBR25F (172.16.1.66, user ccollier) fetched a payload from GitHub, pulled Java dependencies from Maven Central, executed a Java-based STRRAT RAT (bot ID 1BE8292C, reported version 1.6), performed an IP-geolocation self-check via ip-api.com, and began continuous C2 beaconing in the clear to **141.98.10.79:12132**, active for the remainder of the capture with no observed operator commands beyond keep-alive pings.
